definition.text: A hypothecated, or earmarked, tax is one whose revenue is set aside for a particular kind of spending.

facts.text: It departs from the usual practice of paying all government spending out of one consolidated fund.
In strong hypothecation the tax funds only that service and the service is funded only by that tax; otherwise it is weak.
Supporters cite transparency, trust and public acceptance of higher taxes when people see where the money goes.
Critics say spending should follow policy rather than revenue, and earmarking reduces fiscal flexibility.

definition.text: A landfill tax is a charge per tonne or per unit of volume that raises the cost of dumping waste in landfill.

facts.text: It can raise revenue, fund environmental mitigation, or deter landfilling by making better alternatives cheaper by comparison.
Landfilling is discouraged because of landfill gas from biodegradable waste, scarce sites, lost recyclable materials and local opposition.
The UK's landfill tax, introduced in 1996, was its first environmental tax.
By making landfill dearer it creates an incentive to recycle plastics.

definition.text: Optimal tax theory studies how to design taxes that do the most for overall social welfare within economic limits.

facts.text: Taxes are needed to fund public goods and redistribution, but most taxes distort behaviour by making the taxed activity less attractive.
The task is to raise the needed revenue and redistribution while causing as little distortion as possible.
Lump-sum taxes and Pigouvian taxes are thought to distort less; a Pigouvian tax moves consumption toward the efficient level.
Frank Ramsey (1927) proposed that each good's tax should depend on how sensitive its supply and demand are to price.
Optimal taxes should also be fair: equal tax for equal ability to pay, and more tax for those with more ability.

definition.text: A lump-sum tax is a fixed amount that everyone pays regardless of income or assets.

facts.text: Because people cannot change their behaviour to pay less, it creates little excess burden.
It can be regressive, since a fixed amount is a bigger share of a poor person's income.

definition.text: Cost pass-through is the extent to which a business changes its prices when its own costs change.

facts.text: It is measured as a pass-through rate; firms may absorb part of a cost change (rate below 1.0) or amplify it (above 1.0).
When buyers must have a good whatever the price, the whole cost increase reaches consumers; when buyers would leave at any price rise, producers absorb it all.
Pass-through is higher when demand is less sensitive to price and supply more sensitive.
A 2021 study found British Columbia's carbon tax was passed fully into energy prices.
